episodes.183384: The environment was prime for fair weather waterspouts across the southern half of Lake Michigan during the morning hours of September 13, 2023. A pocket of cooler air aloft and warmer water temperatures created unstable conditions over Lake Michigan, with lake breeze convergence and a weak surface trough over the lake providing a focused for showers and a few thunderstorms. Overall, 5 waterspouts were observed up and down the shoreline of Lake Michigan from Milwaukee to Racine.
episodes.183447: Afternoon thunderstorms developed along the Continental Divide and then moved east into the Rio Grande Valley. A strong and slow moving storm caused considerable flash flooding across Albuquerque.
episodes.183580: A frontal system brought a period of heavy rain, flash flooding, and embedded thunderstorms to southern New England from the morning to mid evening. In addition to much tree damage from straight line winds, there was one tornado in Connecticut, 2 in Rhode Island, and 1 in Massachusetts. These all occurred in the afternoon.

episodes.183613: A slow-moving thunderstorm briefly became severe over central Pennington County into north central Custer County, producing hail up to golf ball size along with heavy rainfall. The storm became nearly stationary just west of Hermosa and produced 2 to 5 inches of rainfall in less than 2 hours. Runoff from the heavy rainfall caused several roads to be inundated with water and debris west of Hermosa.
episodes.183624: A slow moving cold front moved into the area during the evening of the 12th into the overnight and early morning hours of the 13th. Moisture pooling ahead of the cold front caused instability to increase in addition to added atmospheric moisture. Showers and thunderstorms developed, and some trained over the same areas resulting in instances of flooding and flash flooding. Central and northeastern Maryland were the areas hardest hit, where moisture and instability was highest.
episodes.183739: A cold front produced a few severe thunderstorms generally near and east of I-95 in Maryland.
episodes.183745: A cold front produced a few thunderstorms resulting in gusty winds over area waterways, especially over the northern Chesapeake Bay.
episodes.184612: A short-wave trough moved across the area during the evening which enhanced thunderstorm strength where the sea breezes converged over a moist and unstable airmass.
episodes.184613: A short-wave trough moved across the area during the evening which enhanced thunderstorm strength where the sea breezes converged over a moist and unstable airmass.
episodes.184774: A brief resurgence of the active pattern resulted in scattered strong thunderstorms which resulted in reports of a landspout, hail, and flash flooding.
episodes.184780: Complex of showers and thunderstorms moved eastward across central Arizona in the early morning hours south of the Mogollon Rim. Another wave of low pressure moved across Arizona for the second day in a row. Low level moisture transport resulted  organized convection along and south of the Mogollon Rim.
episodes.184893: A thunderstorm developed over the Wind River Range and produced a 62 mph wind gust at the Lander Airport.
episodes.185163: Scattered thunderstorms developed across parts of Central Alabama during the afternoon and evening hours on September 12th, producing tree damage in parts of Jefferson, St. Clair, and Randolph counties.
episodes.185259: A slow moving cold front sparked thunderstorm development in the early morning hours on September 13th, 2023. These thunderstorms moved fairly slowly and trained over portions of Southern Connecticut producing flash flooding with rainfall rates of 1-3 inches per hour. Portions of the area picked up 1-2 inches of rainfall in an hour or less. The environment was unstable with 1000 J/kg of SBCAPE and PWATs of 1.7 inches.
episodes.185709: The synoptic pattern was characterized by strong westerly flow aloft situated across most of the Desert Southwest with embedded shortwave energy providing the main source for rising motion. Above normal moisture was present with PWATs in excess of 1.5 across most of central and southwestern AZ. The available moisture in combination with the daytime heating led to the development of moderate instability  with MLCAPE in excess of 1000 J/KG. The strong westerly flow aloft led to strong vertical shear with 0-6 KM shear values ranging between 30-40 knots. All of these factors led to a very favorable environment for the development of strong to severe thunderstorms across portions of south-central AZ. Scattered thunderstorms started to develop by the early afternoon hours of the 12th with multiple rounds continuing into the evening hours. One severe thunderstorm in particular developed near the Buckeye area, became supercellular, and tracked generally eastward affecting areas such as Goodyear, Glendale, Phoenix, Scottsdale, Mesa and Apache Junction, causing extensive straight-line wind damage along its path. Additional thunderstorms developed just east of the Phoenix metro area during the overnight and early morning hours of the 13th, with the main impact being isolated flash flooding.
episodes.185822: A cold front approached from the west with scattered strong to severe thunderstorms developing late in the night on September 12th. Storms produced frequent lightning.
episodes.185823: A strong cold front approached early in the morning on September 13th, with widespread showers and thunderstorms developing. A few strong to severe thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts in parts of the Eastern Shore of Maryland.
episodes.185898: A cold front was first situated to the southeast of the area during the morning, but shifted slightly northward through the day, while an upper level disturbance rotated moved over the region. Residual moisture in the area kept dewpoints elevated throughout the day, and clearing skies led to increasing instability. This set up led to an isolated severe thunderstorm along the southern Blue Ridge in the North Carolina foothills.
episodes.185938: Scattered thunderstorms moved east across Graham and Greenlee counties from the predawn hours through the morning. Additional thunderstorms developed across Cochise, Pima and Pinal counties during the afternoon and moved east or northeast into early evening. Large hail dented vehicles in Kearny.
episodes.186053: Upper level moisture which sheared off from former Pacific Hurricane Jova fueled isolated thunderstorms in the southern Great Basin. One produced flooding.
episodes.186178: A broken line of thunderstorms developed in the late evening hours across the Midlands of South Carolina and moved to the southeast into portions of the Lowcountry. Though these thunderstorms were weakening, they produced strong wind gusts across portions of Colleton County.
episodes.186179: Due to light winds and a warm and humid low-level airmass conditions became favorable for the development of waterspouts along the southeast South Carolina coast. One waterspout was sighted off of Folly Beach.
episodes.186180: Scattered thunderstorms developed in the early evening hours across southeast Georgia ahead of a nearby stationary front. One cluster of thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts and cloud-to-ground lightning strikes across Effingham County.
episodes.186244: Scattered thunderstorms and storm clusters developed across western North Carolina during the late afternoon. A couple of storms produced brief damaging wind gusts in the northern Piedmont.
episodes.186542: A cluster of heavy rain producing thunderstorms along and near a surface low and cold frontal boundary resulted in numerous road closures and roads being washed out on September 13, 2023. Flooding was mostly concentrated within the towns of Washington and Roxbury.

Numerous reports of considerable damage at Falcon Field Airport from a severe microburst. Around 25 airplanes, mostly Cessna small aircraft, were damaged or destroyed, with some flipped over. One aviation flight school lost one third of their fleet, but it is unknown how many aircraft that amounts to. A few pilots reported that even planes with proper tie-downs broke free, with wind eyelets snapping and chains breaking as the planes likely tried to become airborne. Numerous hangars suffered significant damage, with around 90 hangar doors damaged or destroyed. Two World War II era hangars were damaged, with one losing its roof. Another hangar had an entire side wall shorn off. There were several downed trees around the airport, as well as damages to some other airport infrastructure and property, like fencing. A news report nearly three months later stated repairs are still being done and the total damages at the airport is around $7.2 million. An ASOS at Falcon Field Airport did not measure peak wind gusts from this storm due to a loss of power at the airport. Thus, based on damages, winds were estimated around 90 mph. No injuries were reported.

Creeks through town were overflowing across roads at culverts, and in one spot, Kanab Creek was overflowing across the road with water approximately 9 to 12 deep. Dirt roads on the outskirts of town were impassable. Additionally, Kane County Sheriff's office officials reported that several homes had some minor basement flooding. This flooding is the result of strong thunderstorms in the area, with Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor estimates of approximately 0.75 to 1.50 of rainfall in around 3 hours.
A couple of reports of hail to golf ball size in this area.

Flash flooding was reported on Short Creek and its tributaries through the Hilldale and Colorado City area. All creek road crossings were closed for 2 to 3 hours, and the Hilldale Street Creek crossing was heavily damaged and subsequently closed indefinitely until repairs could be made. This flooding is the result of strong thunderstorms which per Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor, produced approximately 3.00 to 4.00 of rainfall, largely within the span of 2 hours, though some of this can likely be attributed to hail contamination. At 6:25 am MST on the 14th, the downstream Fort Pearce Wash gauge recorded a spike in flow to 124 CFS associated with the flood water propagation.
